prompt: In Shared VPC, which project owns the network and its firewall rules?

choices.text: Each service project, for its own subnets
choices.why: The subnets are the host's; the machines are the service project's.

choices.text: The host project, which shares it
choices.why: Right. Service projects put machines in its subnets.

choices.text: The organisation
choices.why: A network belongs to a project, here the host.

choices.text: The billing account
choices.why: Billing accounts pay; they own no networks.

prompt: Why does the planner grant Network User on one subnet rather than on the host project?
hint: What would the project grant cover?

choices.text: Subnet grants are cheaper
choices.why: Roles cost nothing.

choices.text: Network User cannot be granted on a project
choices.why: It can; it would reach too far.

choices.text: It lets the team edit the subnet's range
choices.why: Network User uses a subnet; changing it is networkAdmin.

choices.text: On the project it covers every subnet
choices.why: Right. On one subnet, the team puts machines there and nowhere else.

prompt: A machine that `planner-staging` creates in a subnet of `planner-network` sends a terabyte to Santiago. Which project is billed?

choices.text: planner-staging, which created it
choices.why: Right. The service project pays for its machines and the traffic they send.

choices.text: planner-network, which owns the subnet
choices.why: The network's owner does not pay for others' machines.

choices.text: Both, half each
choices.why: The cost is not split.

choices.text: Whichever project the billing account names first
choices.why: There is no such order.

prompt: Who can make `planner-network` a host project?

choices.text: Any owner of planner-network
choices.why: Making a host needs the Shared VPC Admin role on the tree.

choices.text: A Network User of its subnets
choices.why: That role uses a subnet; it attaches nothing.

choices.text: A Shared VPC Admin
choices.why: Right. `roles/compute.xpnAdmin`, on the organisation or a folder.

choices.text: The billing administrator
choices.why: Billing roles do not touch networks.

prompt: A service project is attached to ___ host project at a time.
The planner creates a peering to the partner's network. When does traffic flow?

choices.text: At once, since the planner created it
choices.why: One side cannot join itself to a network that did not agree.

choices.text: When Google approves the request
choices.why: Google does not approve peerings; the other side does, by making its own.

choices.text: Once the other side makes its own
choices.why: Right. A peering is inactive until both sides have created it.

choices.text: After the next route refresh, within an hour
choices.why: Time is not the condition; the other side is.

prompt: The planner peers with the partner and with analytics. Can the partner reach analytics?

choices.text: Not through the planner
choices.why: Right. They need a peering of their own.

choices.text: Yes, through the planner
choices.why: Routes learned over a peering are not passed on to another peer.

choices.text: Yes, if the planner exports custom routes
choices.why: Peering subnet routes still stop at one hop.

choices.text: Only if all three are in one organisation
choices.why: Organisations do not change transitivity.

prompt: Why can the planner not peer with the company it bought?

choices.text: They are in different organisations
choices.why: Peering works across organisations.

choices.text: The acquired network is in auto mode
choices.why: Its ranges are 10.10.0.0/20 and 192.168.0.0/24, outside the auto block.

choices.text: Peering needs Shared VPC first
choices.why: They are separate features.

choices.text: Their ranges overlap
choices.why: Right. 10.10.0.0/20 is inside the planner's 10.10.0.0/16, and Google refuses the peering.

prompt: After both sides create a peering, the partner's machines still cannot connect to the planner's service. What is missing?

choices.text: A third peering through analytics
choices.why: The two are already peered directly.

choices.text: A firewall rule on the planner's side
choices.why: Right. Firewall rules stay on each side, and the implied deny refuses the rest.

choices.text: Exporting custom routes
choices.why: Subnet routes are exchanged already.

choices.text: Cloud NAT on the partner's side
choices.why: Peering traffic uses internal addresses; NAT is for the internet.

prompt: Why did the planner leave `export_custom_routes` false on the partner peering?
hint: What custom routes does the planner have?

choices.text: So the office route stays the planner's
choices.why: Right. Exported, the partner would learn a route to the planner's office.

choices.text: Exporting routes costs extra per route
choices.why: The setting decides what is learned, not a price.

choices.text: Subnet routes would stop being exchanged
choices.why: Subnet routes are exchanged either way.

choices.text: The partner's network is in another region
choices.why: Networks are global; regions do not enter into it.

prompt: Five networks must all reach each other through peering alone. How many peerings, each counted once for both of its sides, does that take?
Two teams of the same company want their machines in one network, with one firewall run by the network team. Which fits?

choices.text: A peering between their networks
choices.why: That is two networks with two firewalls.

choices.text: A VPN between their projects
choices.why: A VPN joins networks; it does not make one.

choices.text: Shared VPC, with one host
choices.why: Right. One host, the teams as service projects.

choices.text: One project for both teams
choices.why: That shares far more than a network.

prompt: Why is the planner's development network not peered with production?
hint: What would it be the first step towards?

choices.text: Their ranges overlap
choices.why: The planner's ranges were cut not to.

choices.text: To keep test code away from live data
choices.why: Right. A peering would be the first step towards it.

choices.text: Peering is forbidden inside one organisation
choices.why: It is allowed.

choices.text: Development has no network of its own
choices.why: It keeps one in planner-dev.

prompt: Match each neighbour of the planner to how it is joined.

pairs.right: a service project of the host
a peering, with no custom routes
a network of its own, unpeered

right_distractors: a host project of its own partner

prompt: The planner's estate grows to eight networks that must all reach each other. What does the lesson point to?

choices.text: Twenty-eight peerings, kept by hand
choices.why: That works and grows as the square of the networks.

choices.text: One peering to a central network
choices.why: Peering is not transitive, so the spokes would not reach each other.

choices.text: Merging them into one auto mode network
choices.why: Auto mode makes joining harder, not easier.

choices.text: Network Connectivity Center
choices.why: Right. Networks attach as spokes to one hub and reach each other through it.

prompt: Put the steps of joining the acquired company to the planner in order.
items: create the peering on both sides
write firewall rules on each side
trap: Creating the peering before renumbering is the slip: Google refuses it while the ranges overlap.

prompt: A new team in the planner wants staging machines and the right to change the staging subnet's firewall rules. What does the planner's design give them?

choices.text: securityAdmin on the host project
choices.why: That would give them every rule in the shared network.

choices.text: A peering to a network of their own
choices.why: That leaves Shared VPC for a second network to run.

choices.text: networkAdmin on the staging subnet
choices.why: networkAdmin changes networks; firewall rules are securityAdmin's.

choices.text: Network User on the subnet, no more
choices.why: Right. Machines are theirs to place; rules are the host's.
